URL: https://www.iranintl.com/en/202611237477
Iran International

At least five people have died after consuming counterfeit alcoholic drinks in Neyshabur, Shiraz and Marvdasht in recent days, according to official figures.

The number of people poisoned in Neyshabur reached 120, with four deaths, Milad Taqdisi Heydarian, acting deputy for treatment at Neyshabur University of Medical Sciences, said on November 22.

One patient was declared brain-dead and 11 others required intubation, according to the official figures.

Health officials in Shiraz also reported around 30 methanol poisoning cases in Shiraz and Marvdasht, leaving one person dead and four in intensive care.

The poisonings prompted widespread reactions from Iran International's audience, with many arguing that the Islamic Republic's ban on alcohol production, sales and consumption has fueled an unregulated market.

"Look at the result of prohibition. This is how they end up giving people poison," one citizen wrote.

Another criticized those who blamed the victims for drinking alcohol, questioning why Iran does not permit the sale of alcoholic drinks that meet international safety standards.

Several respondents argued that prohibition had failed to stop consumption while removing safeguards against dangerous products.

"People in our country drink alcohol. At least legalize it and regulate it. That would be better than the current situation," one citizen wrote.

"I don't drink, but its import and sale should be legalized," another said.

Fatal alcohol poisonings have repeatedly occurred in Iran. In December 2025, eight people died and one lost their sight after consuming contaminated drinks in separate cases in Iranshahr and Bampur.

Alcohol poisoning accounted for around five percent of 4,232 poisoning-related deaths during the first five months of the Iranian calendar year, according to a forensic medicine report published in October 2025.

Homemade and counterfeit alcoholic drinks were identified as major causes.

Some respondents accused institutions linked to the Islamic Republic, including the Revolutionary Guards, of distributing contaminated drinks.

"The Revolutionary Guards themselves distribute these counterfeit products," one citizen wrote.

Another described those supplying adulterated drinks as "system-affiliated sellers."

One respondent said methanol was advertised on Instagram as "90 percent corn alcohol" for 3000,000 rials per liter and accused the Revolutionary Guards of supplying it.

The actual number of alcohol poisoning cases could be [up to 10 times higher than emergency admission figures https, Deputy Health Minister Alireza Raisi said in October 2025, explaining that some victims avoid treatment because of fear or other reasons.

Methanol poisoning can cause blindness, severe organ damage and death. Health officials in Neyshabur have yet to identify the substance responsible for the latest poisonings.

The deaths have renewed criticism of restrictions that citizens say leave consumers dependent on an unregulated market, with some demanding legalization and quality controls to prevent further fatalities.
